newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. logistics base at Brindisi found sub-standard.
newsitem.headline: U.N. logistics base at Brindisi found sub-standard.

text.p: A U.N. logistics base in Italy that supplies equipment for peacekeeping missions was depicted as woefully inadequate in a critical U.N. watchdog report.

The report circulated on Thursday said the base in Brindisi was incapable of providing adequate support to new missions, and much of the reserve stock of equipment and supplies was in such poor condition it would have to be written off.
The report found stores once valued at $76 million were worth less than $20 million.

The U.N.'s Office of Internal Oversight Services assessment blamed poor organisation and lack of funds and staff for the Logistics Base's failure to "fully meet expectations in performing its approved functions."
It cited failures to receive, inspect, repair and store surplus equipment from closing or downsizing missions, and to maintain reserves in "mission-ready startup kits."

The report by the U.N. equivalent of an inspector-general, Under-Secretary-General Karl Paschke of Germany, also said the base had been "unable to perform a technical evaluation of equipment in stock, had not established proper inventory recording procedures and was only able to provide limited services to new and expanding missions."

In late 1995 the inventory value of the base's equipment and supplies was reduced from an estimated $76 million to a current estimate of $20 million, but the report said the value was "much lower than $20 million."
While the reduction was attributed to write-offs and transfers to other U.N. peacekeping missions, an audit of inventory records led the U.N. oversight office to question their accuracy.
The report found that many vehicles were in extremely poor condition, including some driven as little as 2,500 miles (4,000 km) and that many trucks and light vehicles were only fit for spare parts.

It said containers shipped from the U.N. operation in Somalia containing helicopter and tank spare parts valued at over $6 million had never been opened. One container of helicopter parts valued at more than $1 million was in poor condition and water leakage had damaged some of the contents.
